summary: Explains what it means for a domain name to be reserved for special use, when that is appropriate, and the procedure for doing it. It establishes an IANA registry of such names and seeds it with entries for some already established special domain names. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Some domain names are not meant to be used for real. example.com is for writing documentation, invalid is for names that must never resolve, and localhost always points back at the machine itself. This document says what each of these should do, sets out the questions a new reserved name has to answer, and creates the registry where the list is kept.

subtitle: When a domain name may be reserved for special handling, how to ask for it, and the first names on the list.

tldr.problem: Some domain names, such as example.com or invalid, are meant to behave differently from ordinary names, but RFC 2606 never said whether software should treat them differently, or how.
tldr.mechanism: Any new special name needs a Standards Action or IESG Approval document that answers seven questions about how users, software, DNS servers and registrars must treat it. IANA records the name in a new registry, seeded with the private-address reverse domains, test, localhost, invalid and the example names.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6761 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1918 and RFC 2606, and it establishes the procedure and the registry for future special-use names.

facts.label: Seeded names
facts.value: Private reverse domains, test, localhost, invalid, example names

today: RFC 6761 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1918 and RFC 2606, and the metadata records no document that obsoletes it. It remains the procedure for reserving a special-use domain name and the description of the names already seeded into the IANA registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Certain individual IP addresses and IP address ranges are treated specially by network implementations and, consequently, are not suitable for use as unicast addresses. For example, IPv4 addresses 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 are multicast addresses, with 224.0.0.1 being the all hosts multicast address. Another example is 127.0.0.1, the IPv4 local host address.

Analogous to Special-Use IPv4 Addresses, the Domain Name System has its own concept of reserved names, such as example.com, example.net and example.org, or any name falling under the top-level pseudo-domain invalid. However, Reserved Top Level DNS Names does not state whether implementations are expected to treat such names differently, and if so, in what way. This document specifies under what circumstances special treatment is appropriate, and in what ways.
sections.plainLanguage: Some IP addresses are reserved by protocol, such as the local host address and the multicast range. The Domain Name System had a similar idea, with names like example.com, but nothing said what software was supposed to do with them. This document fills that gap.

sections.title: When a Special Name Is Worth It
sections.content:
When IP multicast was created, implementations had to be updated to understand what an IP multicast address means and what to do with it. Adding IP multicast to a networking stack entailed more than adding the right routing table entries for those addresses. Supporting IP multicast entails some level of commonality that is consistent across all conformant hosts, independent of what networks those hosts may be connected to. It is possible to build a private isolated network using whatever valid unicast IP addresses and routing topology one chooses, regardless of whether those unicast IP addresses are already in use by other hosts on the public Internet, but the IPv4 multicast address 224.0.0.1 is always the all hosts multicast address, and that is not a local decision.

Similarly, if a domain name has special properties that affect the way hardware and software implementations handle the name, and those properties apply universally regardless of what network the implementation may be connected to, then that domain name may be a candidate for having the IETF declare it to be a Special-Use Domain Name and specify what special treatment implementations should give to it. On the other hand, if declaring a given name to be special would result in no change to any implementations, then the name may not be special in any material way, and it may be more appropriate to use the existing DNS mechanisms to provide the desired delegation, data, or lack of data for the name in question. Where the desired behaviour can be achieved via the existing domain name registration processes, that process should be used. Reservation of a Special-Use Domain Name is not a mechanism for circumventing normal domain name registration processes.

The document works this through with a guaranteed-nonexistent name. Suppose an IETF document specified that a particular name is guaranteed to produce an NXDOMAIN result. Such a document falls within the responsibilities of the IETF, which is responsible for protocol rules. The IETF defines the name character set, length limits and syntax, and the fact that in DNS A is equivalent to a. Portions of the namespace created by those rules are given to ICANN to manage, but ICANN is not free to allocate COM and com to two different name servers.

Now suppose a developer used this guaranteed nonexistent name, knowing it is guaranteed to return NXDOMAIN, and the user's DNS server failed to return NXDOMAIN. The developer's software then fails. Who does the user complain to? If the developer cannot depend on the special name to always return NXDOMAIN, then the special name is worthless. For it to have any use it has to be defined to return NXDOMAIN, by protocol, for all installations, not just by ICANN allocation on the public Internet. ICANN has no jurisdiction over how users configure their own private DNS servers, but developers need a protocol specification that states that returning positive answers for the special name is a protocol violation on all networks. Hence, the act of defining such a special name creates a higher-level protocol rule, above ICANN's management of allocable names on the public Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: A name is worth reserving only if every implementation on every network has to behave the same way for it. If reserving the name would change nothing, the ordinary way of delegating and registering a domain is enough. The document's example is a name that must always fail to resolve: for that to be worth anything, the rule has to hold on private networks too, not only on the public Internet, and only the protocol can say so.

sections.title: The Procedure for Reserving a Name
sections.content:
If it is determined that special handling of a name is required in order to implement some desired new functionality, then an IETF Standards Action or IESG Approval specification MUST be published describing the new functionality.

The specification MUST state how implementations determine that the special handling is required for any given name. This is typically done by stating that any fully qualified domain name ending in a certain suffix, that is, falling within a specified parent pseudo-domain, will receive the special behaviour. In effect, this carves off a sub-tree of the DNS namespace in which the modified name treatment rules apply, analogous to how IP multicast or IP link-local addresses carve off chunks of the IP address space in which their respective modified address treatment rules apply.

The specification also MUST state, in each of the seven Domain Name Reservation Considerations categories, what special treatment, if any, is to be applied. If in all seven categories the answer is none, then possibly no special treatment is required, and requesting reservation of a Special-Use Domain Name may not be appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Reserving a name needs a document that has already gone through the IETF process, and that document has to say how an implementation recognises the name in the first place, usually by naming a parent pseudo-domain. It also has to answer the seven questions, and if the answer to all seven is that nothing special happens, the reservation is probably not worth having.

sections.title: The Seven Reservation Considerations
sections.content:
An IETF Standards Action or IESG Approval document specifying some new naming behaviour, which requires a Special-Use Domain Name to be reserved, needs to contain a subsection of the IANA Considerations section titled Domain Name Reservation Considerations, giving answers in seven categories. In the case of algorithmically generated DNS names, the specifying document needs to clearly identify the set of names generated by the algorithm that would require the proposed special treatment.

The seven categories are these. Users: are human users expected to recognize these names as special and use them differently, and in what way? Application software: are writers of application software expected to make their software recognize these names as special and treat them differently, and in what way? For example, if a human user enters such a name, should the application software reject it with an error message?

Name resolution APIs and libraries: are writers of name resolution APIs and libraries expected to make their software recognize these names as special and treat them differently, and if so how? Caching DNS servers: are developers of caching domain name servers expected to make their implementations recognize these names as special and treat them differently, and if so how? Authoritative DNS servers: are developers of authoritative domain name servers expected to make their implementations recognize these names as special and treat them differently, and if so how?

DNS server operators: does this reserved name have any potential impact on DNS server operators? If they try to configure their authoritative DNS server as authoritative for this reserved name, will compliant name server software reject it as invalid, and do operators need to know about that and understand why? Even if the name server software does not prevent them from using the reserved name, are there other ways that it may not work as expected, of which the operator should be aware? DNS Registries and Registrars: how should they treat requests to register this reserved domain name? Should such requests be denied, or allowed only to a specially designated entity?
sections.plainLanguage: The seven questions walk through everyone who touches a domain name: the person typing it, the program they type it into, the library that looks it up, the two kinds of DNS server, the operator who runs them, and the registrar that hands out names. Each has to be told what to do, because a rule that only some of them follow is not a rule.

sections.title: The Initial Registry
sections.content:
The initial IANA Special-Use Domain Names registry contains entries for the private-address reverse-mapping domains and for the existing Reserved Top Level DNS Names. The private-address reverse-mapping domains listed are 10.in-addr.arpa, 21.172.in-addr.arpa, 26.172.in-addr.arpa, 16.172.in-addr.arpa, 22.172.in-addr.arpa, 27.172.in-addr.arpa, 17.172.in-addr.arpa, 30.172.in-addr.arpa, 28.172.in-addr.arpa, 18.172.in-addr.arpa, 23.172.in-addr.arpa, 29.172.in-addr.arpa, 19.172.in-addr.arpa, 24.172.in-addr.arpa, 31.172.in-addr.arpa, 20.172.in-addr.arpa, 25.172.in-addr.arpa and 168.192.in-addr.arpa, together with any names falling within those domains. Users are free to use these names as they would any other reverse-mapping names, but since there is no central authority responsible for use of private addresses, users should be aware that these names are likely to yield different results on different networks. Caching DNS servers should recognize these names as special and should not, by default, attempt to look up NS records for them or otherwise query authoritative DNS servers; instead they should generate immediate responses for all such queries, to avoid unnecessary load on the root name servers. Registries and registrars must not grant requests to register any of these names in the normal way to any person or entity.

The domain test, and any names falling within it, follow the same pattern: caching and authoritative servers should generate immediate negative responses by default, and registries and registrars must not register them normally.

The domain localhost, and any names falling within it, is special in that users may assume that IPv4 and IPv6 address queries for localhost names will always resolve to the respective IP loopback address. Name resolution APIs should recognize localhost names as special and should always return the IP loopback address for address queries and negative responses for all other query types, and should not send queries for localhost names to their configured caching DNS servers. DNS server operators should be aware that the effective data for localhost names is defined by protocol specification and cannot be modified by local configuration.

The domain invalid, and any names falling within it, is special in that users may assume that queries for invalid names will always return NXDOMAIN responses. Name resolution APIs should recognize invalid names as special and should always return immediate negative responses. DNS server operators should be aware that the effective data for invalid names is defined by protocol specification to be nonexistent and cannot be modified by local configuration.

The domains example, example.com, example.net and example.org, and any names falling within those domains, are reserved for use in documentation. Users should understand that example names are reserved for use in documentation, but application software, name resolution APIs, caching DNS servers and authoritative DNS servers should all treat them as ordinary domain names and resolve them normally. Registries and registrars must not grant requests to register example names in the normal way; all example names are registered in perpetuity to IANA, with the WHOIS record for example.com naming the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority as the registrar and listing A.IANA-SERVERS.NET and B.IANA-SERVERS.NET as name servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry starts with the names already in use. The private reverse-mapping domains answer locally, so they should never reach the root servers. test should fail to resolve. localhost should always resolve to the machine itself, and invalid should always fail. The example names are the opposite: they are reserved for documentation, and they resolve normally like any other domain.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document outlines the circumstances in which reserving a domain name for special use is appropriate, and the procedure for having that Special-Use Domain Name recorded by IANA. Any document requesting such a Special-Use Domain Name needs to contain an appropriate Security Considerations section which describes any security issues relevant to that special use.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC itself adds no new security risk. It does insist that any document asking for a reserved name must say what the security consequences are, because a name that resolves somewhere unexpected, or that silently means something different, is a risk the author has to own.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has created a new registry of Special-Use Domain Names, initially populated with the private-address reverse-mapping domains and the Reserved Top Level DNS Names outlined above.

When IANA receives a request to record a new Special-Use Domain Name, it should verify, in consultation with the IESG, that the IETF Standards Action or IESG Approval document includes the required Domain Name Reservation Considerations section stating how the special meaning of this name affects the behavior of hardware, software and humans in the seven categories. If IANA and the IESG determine that special handling of the name is appropriate, IANA should record the Special-Use Domain Name, and a reference to the specification that documents it, in the registry.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the list, and it starts with the names already covered by this document. Before adding a new name, IANA checks with the IESG that the document behind it really did answer all seven questions, and only then records the name and a reference to the specification.

viz.caption: The seven questions a reservation document must answer

items.title: Users
items.text: Are human users expected to recognize these names as special and use them differently?

items.title: Application software
items.text: Should software recognise these names, and should it reject them with an error message?

items.title: Name resolution APIs and libraries
items.text: Should the code that turns a name into an address treat these names differently?

items.title: Caching DNS servers
items.text: Should a caching server answer these names itself instead of asking upstream?

items.title: Authoritative DNS servers
items.text: Should an authoritative server recognise these names as special?

items.title: DNS server operators
items.text: Does the name affect how an authoritative server is configured, and will software refuse it?

items.title: DNS registries and registrars
items.text: Should requests to register the name be denied, or allowed only to a designated entity?
